Monthly mean at Mauna Loa, Hawaii
Global mean from satellite altimetry, seasons removed
Extent each September, the yearly low

Carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere. Since 1958 it has been measured on the slopes of Mauna Loa, far from local sources, in parts per million (ppm) of dry air. It rises and falls a little each year as northern forests grow and shed their leaves, and climbs year after year because of fossil fuels. Before the industrial age it stood at about 280 ppm. This chart starts in May 1974, with NOAA\'s own measurements.

How much warmer or cooler each month was across the land and oceans than the average of 1951–1980. NASA\'s Goddard Institute for Space Studies combines thousands of weather stations, ships and buoys into one global value. Single months jump around with weather and El Niño; the long climb since the 1970s is the warming.

Satellites have measured the height of the ocean surface since late 1992: TOPEX/Poseidon, then the Jason missions and Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich. The sea rises as ocean water warms and expands and as glaciers and ice sheets melt. The yearly ups and downs of the seasons are removed. NOAA updates this record irregularly, so its latest value can be months old.

Arctic sea ice is frozen ocean water that grows each winter and melts each summer, reaching its smallest extent in September. Extent is the ocean area with at least 15 % ice cover, measured by satellites since 1978. Less ice leaves darker water that absorbs more sunlight, which warms the Arctic further.
Dr. Xin Lan, NOAA/GML (gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/). Monthly mean CO₂ at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii.
